title: Living in a New City: Rustam's First Month
paragraphs: When Rustam Seilov arrived in Uralsk from Aktobe last September, he had a map on his phone, a packed rucksack, and absolutely no idea where anything was. He knew WKU was somewhere in the northern part of the city. He knew his dormitory was at the end of a long street. Beyond that, the city was a blank.

"The first day was genuinely disorienting," he remembers. "I walked out of the dormitory, turned left, and immediately ended up in a car park. I turned around, went back past the main entrance, and walked along the side of the main building. I had no idea whether I was heading towards the campus or away from it." He eventually found the central courtyard by following a group of third-year students.

The second challenge was the bus system. Rustam needed to get to a pharmacy — he had arrived with a cold — and the nearest one was in the city centre. He stood at the stop opposite the main gate for twenty minutes, watching buses go past without getting on any of them. "I didn't know which number to take, and I was too embarrassed to ask," he admits. "Eventually a woman asked me if I was lost. I said yes. She pointed me towards Bus 5 and said it would take me past the main market and through the shopping district."

Getting off at the right stop was the next problem. "I was looking out of the window and trying to match what I saw to the map on my phone," Rustam says. "We went over a bridge, past a large church, and then round a roundabout before I recognised the mosque I'd seen in photos. I got off there." The pharmacy was across the street from the mosque, set back slightly from the pavement. He found it.

By the end of the first week, Rustam had learned the bus routes through trial and error. He had walked along the river twice. He had discovered a small café tucked between two apartment blocks, about ten minutes on foot from the dormitory, where the coffee was excellent and the WiFi was reliable. "That café became my second home," he says.

The second week brought new discoveries. He found that by cutting through the university garden and going along the path behind the sports hall, he could get to the library in six minutes instead of twelve. He discovered that there was a shortcut through an archway on Dostyq Avenue that led directly into the market. And he found the city's best shashlyk restaurant — completely by accident, by going down the wrong street.

"By the end of the first month, I knew Uralsk better than I knew Aktobe," he says. This is probably an exaggeration. But the feeling is real: a city that is walked, not just visited, becomes familiar in a way that no map can fully capture. You know which doorways are sheltered from the wind. You know which streets have the best light in the evening. You know which routes have interesting things to look at and which are purely functional. This knowledge is not written anywhere. It is built, step by step, on foot.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Do you remember your first week in Uralsk? Was it confusing?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Very. I kept going past the right bus stop because all the streets looked the same at first.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Me too. I went over the wrong bridge once and ended up completely on the wrong side of the river.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: At least you explored! I was too scared to go anywhere alone for the first week.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I didn't really have a choice — I needed a pharmacy. Necessity is a good teacher.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: How long before the city felt familiar?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: About three weeks. After that, I stopped looking at maps completely.
